newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-FRENCHMAN WENGER BACKS ENGLAND'S 2006 WORLD CUP BID.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-FRENCHMAN WENGER BACKS ENGLAND'S 2006 WORLD CUP BID.

text.p: Arsenal's French manager Arsene Wenger said on Tuesday he believed the 2006 World Cup finals should be staged in England and said he thoroughly supported the English bid to host the finals.
"Something special exists here in England as far as football is concerned, and I believe it is right that the World Cup should be held here.

"By 2006 it will be 40 years since England last staged the World Cup and I think that after that amount of time it should return to the country where football was created," he told an audience of soccer celebrities, senior officials and journalists at a dinner hosted by the English Football Association and British Government.
"I am backing the F.A.'s bid 100 per cent. Football is my passion, my life, I am grateful to England to be working here and it is my duty to back their bid for the World Cup."

Wenger could be seen as something as a lucky omen by the English as he was working at Monaco in France when they won the right to stage the 1998 finals and was coaching in Japan when they were jointly awarded the 2002 finals with South Korea.
"I hope I am a lucky omen for England" he joked, "but my contract with Arsenal runs out in 1999 and the decision won't be taken until 2000."
Wenger, who joined Arsenal in October was the guest speaker at the dinner, held the night before the bid is officially launched by British Prime Minister John Major.
Sports minister Iain Sproat told guests: "I am sure anybody who has seen the F.A.'s plans will have been impressed by the outstanding style and professionalism of them.
"That is why the Government is backing the F.A. 100 per cent in its effort to bring football's greatest tournament back to these shores for the first time in 40 years.
"Our aim is to make the World Cup in 2006 a tournament to remember.
"The stadia we have in England are second to none in terms of comfort and safety and the atmosphere for fans.
"The jewel in the crown is Wembley where so many of the game's greatest players have delighted us over the years.
"But we do not expect to live on our reputation alone which is why we are transforming Wembley into what will undoubtedly be one of the finest stadiums in the world.
"There can be no better stage for footballers to realise their dream of playing a World Cup final."
It was a busy day for those concerned with the World Cup finals in nine years time.

Earlier on Tuesday, Alec McGivan, the director of England's 2006 campaign, said he thought it was unlikely that England and Germany, the rival European bids for the finals, would ever act as co-hosts as Japan and South Korea will do in 2002.
"It has been mentioned to us a number of times but frankly I don't think it is an option," he said.
"I'm sure that if the bids from England and Germany were so strong that no one could choose between them, then it might be a possibilty.
"But so much would have to happen before that ever became an eventuality. I can't see it materialising."
McGivan's remarks followed developments last week which he admitted "seriously disrupted our strategic thinking on the bid".
Those developments began when UEFA, European soccer's ruling body, sent a surprise fax to the English F.A. saying UEFA would be supporting only Germany's bid to stage the finals.
Intense lobbying followed with UEFA general secretary Gerhard Aigner meeting English officials in London last Friday to say that UEFA would be considering bids by both England and Germany after all.

Bidding nations must submit their documents to FIFA, world soccer's governing body, by September 1999, with FIFA's 24-man executive committee deciding which country will stage the 2006 World Cup in June 2000.
"McGivan said: "During our bidding process we are not going to play down or be negative about any other nation's bid. We are going to emphasise what England has to offer.

"There are six good reasons why England should stage the World Cup -- It is the birthplace of the game; Euro 96 was an outstanding success; England's grounds are now the finest in the world; the rebuilt Wembley Stadium will perhaps be the finest football stadium in the world; there is a unique atmosphere at games in England and England is a great place to visit."

The English F.A., backed by both the Conservative government and Labour opposition, are budgeting between eight and 10 million pounds sterling ($12.8 and $16 million) over the next three years in their efforts to bring the World Cup back to England for the first time since 1966.
Despite the momentum generated in London, England's bid has many obstacles to overcome if it is to succeed.
UEFA president Lennart Johansson hinted on Tuesday that he would still be backing Germany for the finals, despite the fact UEFA have publicly stated they will consider both bids.

Johansson said in an interview with the German agency SID: "The members of the executive committee know what they wanted. I can't say whether anybody is going to change their mind. I have to remain objective.
"But that doesn't mean I'm changing my mind. I know what decision I made and I know who was there."

As well as England and Germany a number of other countries are expected to bid for the finals including Australia, Morocco, South Africa, Egypt with possible joint bids coming from Peru and Ecuador and Argentina and Brazil.
